title: Divisibility Rules OQ-01: Extensions with Truncation, Grouping, and Casting Out Nines
description: A self-contained extension of the divisibility rules gallery adding: the divisibility-by-11 alternating digit sum rule (fully proved), the divisibility-by-13 truncation method (add 4 times the last digit), multi-digit grouping rules for 37, 27, 99, 101, and 999 (sum of consecutive k-digit blocks), a general last-k-digit framework unifying all power-of-2 and power-of-5 rules, divisibility by 16 and 32 via last 4 and 5 decimal digits, casting out nines for both addition and multiplication, and an error-detection theorem. All results are fully machine-verified.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: Self-contained alternating digit sum framework with simplified modEq proof (no case split on b < 2 needed)
Divisibility by 11 as an iff form: 11 | (n - altDigitSum 10 n)
General dvd_iff_dvd_mod theorem unifying all last-k-digit rules as a single theorem
Casting out nines: addition, multiplication, and error detection theorem
Cross-base digit sum rules: 3, 5, 15 in hexadecimal; 3, 5 in other bases

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules have a long history intertwined with practical arithmetic. Casting out nines appears in Hindu-Arabic mathematics by the 9th century (al-Khwarizmi's arithmetic) and was the standard self-checking method for multiplication until the 20th century. The alternating digit sum rule for 11 was codified in the Middle Ages. The truncation method for 7 (subtract twice the last digit) was popularized in modern mathematics textbooks; the analogous method for 13 (add four times the last digit) is its algebraic twin, arising from $10 \cdot 4 \equiv 1 \pmod{13}$. The multi-digit grouping rules (37, 27, 999, 99, 101) are straightforward applications of the congruence $10^k \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ for appropriate $k$; their occurrence in recreational mathematics goes back at least to the 19th century. The last-$k$-digit framework for powers of 2 and 5 (divisibility by 2, 4, 5, 8, 16, 25, 32, 125) has been part of elementary arithmetic curricula for centuries, but the uniform Lean proof via the single dvd_iff_dvd_mod theorem gives it a clean algebraic foundation. The present collection unifies all these rules under two algebraic principles: (1) $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$ gives alternating sums, (2) $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ gives direct sums, and (3) $d \mid m$ gives last-$k$-digit rules.
overview.problemStatement: Extend the base divisibility rules collection with: (1) divisibility by 11 proved as an iff theorem via alternating digit sums; (2) divisibility by 13 via the truncation method; (3) divisibility by 37, 27, 99, 101, and 999 via digit-group sums; (4) a unified general framework dvd_iff_dvd_mod for all last-k-digit rules; (5) casting out nines with error detection.
overview.proofStrategy: The alternating digit sum proof uses induction on the digit list, exploiting that b ≡ -1 (mod d) implies each power of b alternates sign mod d. The general dvd_iff_dvd_mod is proved via Euclidean division: if d | m, then n = m·(n/m) + (n mod m) and d | m·(n/m), so d | n iff d | (n mod m). The truncation rules for 7 and 13 use the identity 10·(q ± c·r) = n ± k·r where k is divisible by the target, then cancel 10 using IsCoprime. Casting out nines follows from the standard Nat.add_mod and Nat.mul_mod identities.
keyInsights: The general dvd_iff_dvd_mod theorem subsumes all specific last-k-digit rules (2, 4, 5, 8, 16, 25, 32, 125) as corollaries with a single uniform proof, reducing multiple textbook facts to one Euclidean-division argument.

The 13-truncation rule (add 4× last digit) is the additive counterpart of the 7-truncation rule (subtract 2× last digit): both choose $c$ so that $10c \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{d}$, enabling cancellation of the factor of 10 via IsCoprime.

The digit-grouping rules for 37, 27, and 999 all follow from $10^3 = 1000 \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, which means summing three-digit blocks is enough — exactly the same mechanism as casting out nines, just with a different base.

Casting out nines error detection works because the map $n \mapsto n \bmod 9$ is a ring homomorphism, so any computation that is wrong mod 9 is definitely wrong — but passing the mod-9 check does not guarantee correctness (false positive rate $1/9$).

The alternating sum and direct sum rules are dual: $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ gives the direct digit sum, $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$ gives the alternating sum. The single framework ofDigits_modEq_alternatingDigitSum handles the $b \equiv -1$ case uniformly.

The cross-base rules (7 in octal, 3/5 in hexadecimal, 4 in base 5) reveal that divisibility is a property of a number independent of its representation — the rules change form but the underlying congruence is always $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$.

conclusion.summary: This OQ-01 extension proves 41 theorems extending the base divisibility rules collection. The general dvd_iff_dvd_mod theorem provides a unified foundation for all last-k-digit rules, while the alternating sum and truncation methods cover divisibility by 7, 11, and 13. The casting out nines module provides both the arithmetic preservation theorems and a practical error-detection theorem.
conclusion.implications: The generalization of last-k-digit rules to a single theorem demonstrates the power of modular arithmetic abstraction. The simultaneous coverage of divisibility by 7, 11, and 13 through the truncation/alternating-sum methods reflects the algebraic unity behind these seemingly disparate rules — all exploiting coprimality of 10 with the target divisor.
openQuestions: Formalize the divisibility rule for 7 via alternating three-digit blocks (using 1000 ≡ -1 mod 7), unifying with the DivisibilityByThreeOQ02 approach
Prove that for every d coprime to 10, there exists a base B (a power of 10) such that either d | (sum of B-ary digits of n) or d | (alternating sum of B-ary digits of n)
Extend the error-detection theorem to a probabilistic version: a random arithmetic mistake is detected by casting out nines with probability 8/9

sections.title: Part I: Alternating Digit Sum Framework
sections.summary: Defines alternatingDigitSum as a recursive function on List ℕ and proves the key inductive lemma alternatingDigitSum_cons. The theorem ofDigits_modEq_alternatingDigitSum establishes that when b ≡ -1 (mod d), Nat.ofDigits b l ≡ alternatingDigitSum l (mod d), and modEq_alternating_digits_sum lifts this to a statement about natural numbers n.

sections.title: Part II: Divisibility by 11
sections.summary: Proves eleven_dvd_iff: 11 ∣ (n - altDigitSum 10 n) for all n : ℕ, using the fact that 10 ≡ -1 (mod 11). Three examples confirm the rule for 121, 1001, and 123.

sections.title: Part III: Truncation Rules for 7 and 13
sections.summary: Proves thirteen_dvd_truncation (13 ∣ n ↔ 13 ∣ (n/10 + 4·(n%10))) and seven_dvd_truncation (7 ∣ n ↔ 7 ∣ (n/10 - 2·(n%10))) using the IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left method. Both proofs use push_cast + omega for the key algebraic identity.

sections.title: Part IV: Digit Sum Rules in Various Bases
sections.summary: A private helper dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum wraps Nat.modEq_digits_sum into an iff form. 14 theorems instantiate it: divisibility by 3, 9 (base 10); 37, 27, 999 (base 1000); 99 (base 100); 101 (base 10000); 7 (octal); 3, 5, 15 (hexadecimal); 3 (base 4); 5 (base 6); 4 (base 5); 8 (base 9); 13 (base 14).

sections.title: Part V: General Last-k-Digit Framework
sections.summary: The theorem dvd_iff_dvd_mod (if d ∣ m then d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (n%m)) gives the uniform foundation for all last-k-digit rules. Seven corollaries cover divisibility by 2, 5 (last 1 digit), 4, 25 (last 2 digits), 8, 125 (last 3 digits), 16 (last 4 digits), 32 (last 5 digits).

sections.title: Part VI: Combined Coprime Factorization Rules
sections.summary: coprime_mul_dvd_iff proves d₁·d₂ ∣ n ↔ d₁ ∣ n ∧ d₂ ∣ n for coprime d₁, d₂. Instantiated for 6 (=2·3), 12 (=4·3), 15 (=3·5).

sections.title: Part VII: Casting Out Nines
sections.summary: Proves casting_out_nines_add, casting_out_nines_mul (one-line applications of Nat.add_mod, Nat.mul_mod), and the error detection theorem casting_nines_error_detect. Part VIII verifies examples: 123·456 ≡ 56088 (mod 9), 12·13 ≠ 155.

sections.title: Part VIII-IX: Verification Examples and Summary
sections.summary: Eight example computations confirm the rules in practice. The oq01_rules_verification theorem bundles 7 specific divisibility facts into a single conjunction proved by native_decide. Summary #check commands expose all key theorem names.
